request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Patient Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Patient Name]
Admission Date: [Admission Date]
Discharge Date: [Discharge Date]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital due to lower extremity swelling and pain for four days. Physical examination revealed left lower limb pitting edema and calf tenderness. Color Doppler ultrasound showed an extensive DVT affecting the common iliac, external iliac and common femoral vein as well as superficial femoral down to popliteal vein. Treatment included bed rest, elevation with bandaging of left leg, and low molecular weight heparin injections. Investigations revealed no underlying etiology. Abdominal and pelvic US and CT scan showed an impacting stone and a severe left hydroureteronephrosis with almost lost of cortical thickness. Percutaneous nephrostomy was performed to decompress the hydronephrotic kidney. JJ stent was inserted and subsequently removed. Six weeks later, Doppler US showed complete recanalization of the superficial femoral, popliteal as well as the proximal segment of deep veins of the leg but common iliac, external iliac and common femoral veins and proximal superficial femoral vein were still partially thrombosed. Through pneumatic lithotripsy, the stone was fragmented under spinal anesthesia. Three months after that, Doppler US showed complete recanalization of iliac vessels.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment:
Treatment included bed rest, elevation with bandaging of left leg, and low molecular weight heparin injections. Percutaneous nephrostomy was performed to decompress the hydronephrotic kidney. JJ stent was inserted and subsequently removed. Pneumatic lithotripsy was performed to fragment the stone under spinal anesthesia. The patient was discharged on oral anticoagulation in the form of rivaroxaban 20 mg daily.

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to have regular follow-up visits with their healthcare provider.

Signed by: [Healthcare Provider Name and Title]

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The admission was for left leg swelling and pain, and the extensive DVT was the condition that prompted it. Investigation then found an obstructing ureteric stone with severe hydroureteronephrosis, which was thought to be the underlying cause of the DVT through compression of the iliac veins or a hypercoagulable state. The main treatment was anticoagulation, with the stone managed afterwards.

The principal diagnosis is the condition established after study to be chiefly responsible for the admission. The patient was admitted for the DVT, which was investigated and treated first. The stone was an incidental finding, though it was treated later. The DVT was extensive, involving the iliofemoral veins, so the code is I80 (phlebitis and thrombophlebitis) or, in ICD-10-AM, I82 (other venous embolism and thrombosis). Acute DVT of the deep veins of the lower limb codes to I80.2 in ICD-10 and in ICD-10-AM. In ICD-10-AM, I80 includes "Phlebitis and thrombophlebitis" with I80.1 femoral vein and I80.2 other deep vessels of the lower extremities, and DVT is coded there. I82 covers other venous embolism and thrombosis, such as the vena cava, renal vein and portal vein, so it does not apply here. The iliofemoral DVT therefore goes to I80.

CODE: I80
